metaDescription: Five plant caddies under $30 compared on 240 to 500 lb ratings, one vs many locking casters, wood vs nylon and adjustable sizing for heavy deck planters.
introParagraphs: This budget is where plant caddies stop being only for houseplants. Add a little to the cheapest tier and you reach a 500 lb nylon and steel model made for decks and patios, which changes who the guide is for. The question is no longer just whether a base rolls, but how many wheels lock, what the wheels are made of, and whether the platform fits a wide pot.

We evaluated five distinct caddies: the Lissomballon 12 inch wood pair, the Bamworld 12 inch wood pair, the VANCASTLE adjustable 15 to 22 inch frame, the WanderingDonkey 14 inch plastic caddie and the Bosmere 16 inch caddie with a 500 lb listed capacity. Pack sizes of the same model and size variants were skipped, so every entry is a different design.
The picks are compared by capacity, platform size, lock count and the materials the listings name, with notes on what stepping past this budget adds.

products.name: Bosmere 16 Inch Plant Caddie, 500 lb Capacity
products.description:
The Bosmere Down Under Plant Caddie is sold as a 16 inch heavy duty roller with a listed 500 lb capacity. The listing says it works with all pots regardless of shape or size and describes nylon and steel wheels for smooth rolling on a deck or patio.

The headline spec is the capacity, which is double the Lissomballon at 240 lbs and above the VANCASTLE's roughly 440 to 450 lbs. The tradeoff is locking, because the listing mentions a single locking caster, so it will hold less firmly than a model with several locks. For a heavy ceramic planter on a flat deck, that may be acceptable, while on a slope it is not.

In ownership, a 16 inch footprint suits big terracotta and resin pots, and the metal in the wheels suggests it is meant for rough outdoor surfaces. It is the largest fixed caddy in this lineup, so it is the answer if the 14.17 inch WanderingDonkey is too small. If you want more than one lock on a smaller pot, the Lissomballon pair is the better pick. The Bosmere also helps with tall plants, where a stable wide base matters more than a light one.
products.bestFor: Heavy decks and patios with large, heavy pots.
pros: Listed 500 lb capacity is the highest here
Nylon and steel wheels roll on rough ground
Large 16 inch size fits wide pots
Works with pots of any shape

products.name: VANCASTLE Adjustable Plant Caddy, 15 to 22 Inch

specList.label: Capacity
specList.value: 450 lbs in title, 440 lbs in text

products.description:
The VANCASTLE is a frame built from ABS panels and stainless steel tubes that you stretch to fit your pot, anywhere between 15 and 22 inch. The listing calls the ABS durable and odorless, says the wheels lock, and cites a capacity of 450 lbs in the title and 440 lbs in one line of text.

Its size range is the main reason to buy. A 12 inch round tray cannot carry a wide planter, and even the Bosmere stops at 16 inch, while this frame goes to 22 inch. It also suits square pots better, since you can set the frame to the actual width of the base instead of overhanging a circle.

In ownership, tighten the tube connections and check the frame sits level after you extend it. Compared with the Bosmere, you get a wider range and more locking wheels stated, but a lower capacity and more parts. Compared with the 12 inch wooden pairs, it costs more but suits much larger pots. If you ever repot into a bigger container, the frame can simply be lengthened.
products.bestFor: Wide, square or mixed size planters.
pros: Lockable wheels stated in the listing
cons: Two capacity figures in the listing
More parts than a one piece caddie
Needs setup and a level check

products.name: WanderingDonkey 14 Inch Plant Caddie
products.description:
The WanderingDonkey is a one piece plastic caddie made from toughened tempered plastic with a frosted surface. It measures 14.17 inch outside and 12.68 inch inside, is rated for 265 lbs and needs no assembly. The listing says it rolls over hardwood, concrete and carpet.

This is the simplest caddie in the guide. Nothing needs to be bolted on, so the usual failure point of a cheaper unit, a wheel that loosens, is removed from the setup. It is a good match for a mid sized pot on a hard floor. The listing does not mention wheel locks, and the saucer has no drain holes, so use it for pots that you water over a sink or with a catch tray.

In ownership, the lack of locks is the main compromise. Compared with the Bosmere, you give up capacity and a locking caster, and compared with the Lissomballon you give up two locking wheels for 25 lbs more rating and a bigger platform. If your floors are level, it is a clean solution.
products.bestFor: Mid weight pots on level hard floors, without any setup.
pros: 265 lbs rating suits mid weight pots
Rolls on hardwood, concrete and carpet
14.17 inch outer diameter fits wider bases
cons: No drain holes in the saucer

products.name: Lissomballon 12 Inch Wood Plant Caddy, 2 Pack
products.description:
The Lissomballon pair gives you two 12 inch round wood caddies with 360 degree lockable casters, rated at 240 lbs each. The frame is described as carbon wood, and the listing says it works with small succulent pots up to large heavy planters, and even laundry bins or trash cans.

At this budget it is the cheapest way to get locking wheels on two bases. That matters for indoor plants on slopes or near doors, where a pot that creeps is annoying. The platform is only 12 inch, so wider pots are out, and the wood should sit under a saucer so that water does not collect against it.

In ownership, the caddies are lightweight and easy to store, and the spare lets you rotate plants for light. Against the Bosmere, it offers more locks but only about half the capacity. Against the VANCASTLE, it is smaller but far simpler and cheaper per caddy.
products.bestFor: Two indoor pots that need locking wheels.
pros: Fits pots from small to large at 12 inch
cons: Wood needs a saucer for water
Setup is required for the casters

products.name: Bamworld 12 Inch Plant Caddy, 2 Pack
products.description:
The Bamworld two pack is a 12 inch round wood tray with metal connections and rolling casters that the listing says lock. It describes 360 degree mobility and a sturdy plant stand made from premium wood. The product is aimed at indoor pots of various sizes.

This is the look first option among the pairs. The wood tray suits a living room, and the locking casters keep a plant where you put it. The listing does not state a load rating, so check the product page before placing a heavy planter on it. For a guaranteed number, the Lissomballon states 240 lbs.

In ownership, treat it like any wooden stand, keeping it dry and using a saucer. It is nearly interchangeable with the Lissomballon in size, so the choice comes down to the rating statement and the look. If your pot is wider than 12 inch, step up to the WanderingDonkey or VANCASTLE.
products.bestFor: Decorative indoor setups with light to medium pots.
cons: No load rating in the listing text

buyingCriteria.explanation: A fully watered pot is much heavier than the empty pot, so rate by wet weight and add a 20 percent margin. A 16 inch ceramic planter can pass 150 lbs after watering. The Lissomballon is rated for 240 lbs, the WanderingDonkey for 265 lbs, the VANCASTLE for roughly 440 to 450 lbs and the Bosmere for 500 lb. Heavy concrete or stone pots call for the last two. As an example, a 16 inch planter with about 60 lbs of wet soil and a 15 lb shrub is a 75 lb load, which every pick handles easily.

A caddy with one locking caster can still pivot around the locked wheel, while two or more locks hold the pot in place. Locks matter most on slopes, decks with a tilt, and near doors. The Lissomballon, Bamworld and VANCASTLE state locks on the casters. The Bosmere lists one locking caster and the WanderingDonkey does not mention any. If you must use a single lock, park the caddy so the locked wheel is on the downhill side. That small habit keeps the pivot from drifting.

Hard plastic wheels roll fine on smooth floors but can stick on rough pavers and gaps. Nylon and steel wheels handle outdoor texture better, and soft rubber protects delicate floors. The Bosmere lists nylon and steel wheels, which is why it is the deck choice. For indoor wood floors, use a tray with a saucer or felt pad. Gaps between deck boards and paver joints are where small hard wheels get stuck, so larger wheels help. Check the wheel diameter on the product page, because the listings here do not state it for every model. Rolling a pot slowly is safer than a quick push, whichever wheel you pick.

The pot base should sit fully on the platform with about an inch of clearance. Round caddies under square pots leave corners unsupported. The wood pairs are 12 inch, the WanderingDonkey is 12.68 inch inside, the Bosmere is 16 inch and the VANCASTLE adjusts from 15 to 22 inch. Measure the base, not the rim. Leave an inch of clearance so you can still reach the saucer edge. A very wide platform under a small pot raises the tipping risk. The VANCASTLE avoids this because you can pull the frame in to match the base.

Wood can swell with standing water, while plastic, ABS, nylon and steel suit outdoor use more easily. The two wood pairs belong indoors with a saucer. The WanderingDonkey, VANCASTLE and Bosmere are better fits for patios and decks. Sun exposure can fade plastic over time. Sun and rain age plastic over several seasons, so treat any outdoor caddy as a consumable. A winter move into a garage prolongs life. Wood caddies should never sit in a wet saucer.

Past this budget you can expect more wheels, larger sizes and stronger frames. This band already includes a 500 lb rated model, so the step up is mostly about extra locks or very large pots. If your plant exceeds 22 inch across, you will likely need a custom or multi caster platform. Typical upgrades include extra casters on the corners, a rim to hold the pot, and wheels that are larger in diameter. Expect those on caddies above this budget, and only pay for them if you move a heavy pot often.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity and rating clarity
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated loads from 240 lbs on the Lissomballon to 500 lb on the Bosmere. We noted where a listing gives conflicting figures, as the VANCASTLE does with 450 and 440 lbs, and where it gives none, as with the Bamworld. Clear numbers were credited. We treated a margin of at least 20 percent below the stated rating as a reasonable working limit. That puts the practical ceiling for the Lissomballon near 190 lbs.

howWeEvaluated.title: Wheel and lock design
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at wheel material and how many wheels lock. The Bosmere is the only one naming nylon and steel wheels, and the Lissomballon and Bamworld state locking casters. The WanderingDonkey lacks any lock mention. We also noted that a caddy with only one stated lock, such as the Bosmere, scores lower for slopes than the Lissomballon despite a higher rating.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit and platform size
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched each platform to common pot sizes, from 12 inch to 22 inch. The VANCASTLE leads on range, the Bosmere on the largest fixed size. Pots wider than the platform scored as unsafe. Where only an outer diameter is given, we flagged that the usable platform is smaller. The WanderingDonkey is the one entry that lists both numbers.

howWeEvaluated.title: Material and weather suitability
howWeEvaluated.description: Wood suits indoor use, while ABS, tempered plastic and nylon steel suit patios. We considered the care each material needs. The wood pairs scored lower for outdoor use. We noted that material also drives weight, since a plastic caddie is easier to carry to a storage shed than a steel framed model.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value inside the cap
howWeEvaluated.description: Five different tiers fit under the cap, from a cheap locking pair to the heavy duty Bosmere. We weighed what each gives up. Positioning comes from listing specs and buyer feedback, not hands on measurement. We also asked whether a larger rating was usable in practice, because a 500 lb caddy is wasted under a 40 lb pot.

faq.q: Which plant caddy under this budget is best?
faq.a: The Bosmere 16 inch is best for heavy deck planters with a 500 lb listed capacity. The Lissomballon pair is best for indoor plants that need locking wheels. The VANCASTLE is best when your pots are wide or square. If you are unsure, measure your pot base first, since that narrows the field faster than any rating.

faq.q: How much weight can a plant caddy hold?
faq.a: In this lineup the range runs from 240 lbs on the Lissomballon to 500 lb on the Bosmere. The WanderingDonkey is 265 lbs and the VANCASTLE is roughly 440 to 450 lbs. Include the wet soil and the water when you add up the load.

It keeps a pot from rolling away, but the pot can still pivot around the locked wheel. For a slope or a place people pass by, choose a caddy with more locks, such as the Lissomballon or VANCASTLE. On a flat deck one lock is usually acceptable. Check whether the locked wheel faces the slope, since the downhill side matters most.

They can on a covered porch, but they are not ideal for rain. Wood swells with standing water, so use a saucer and keep it dry. For open decks, the plastic or nylon models are the safer choice. A cover or a roof overhang makes a big difference to wood caddies.

faq.q: Do I need to assemble these?
faq.a: The WanderingDonkey needs no assembly. The wood pairs and the VANCASTLE need setup, and the VANCASTLE has the most parts. Tighten the casters after the first week. Allow ten minutes for the casters and a screwdriver for the frame models.

faq.q: Why not buy the biggest caddy?
faq.a: A platform much larger than the pot base wastes space and can tip when the load sits off center. Match the platform to the base. The VANCASTLE helps when sizes vary because it adjusts. As a rule, keep the platform within an inch or two of the pot base.
Buyers sometimes report wheels that loosen or detach under heavy use. Stay below the rating and check the wheel mounts. A higher rated model gives more margin.
